author: bereshit-rabbah

lemma.he: אֲבָל אֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ בְּאֵיזֶה מֵהֶם חָפֵץ
lemma.en: but I do not know which of them he desires

original.text: רבי אבהו ור' חייא רבה רבי אבהו אמר מתחלת ברייתו של עולם צפה הקדוש ברוך הוא במעשיהן של צדיקים ומעשיהן של רשעים הדא הוא דכתיב (תהלים א, ו): "כי יודע ה' דרך צדיקים וגו'". "וְהָאָרֶץ הָיְתָה תֹהוּ וָבֹהוּ" אלו מעשיהן של רשעים "וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹהִים יְהִי אוֹר" אלו מעשיהן של צדיקים אבל איני יודע באיזה מהם חפץ אם במעשה אלו ואם במעשה אלו כיון דכתיב "וַיַּרְא אֱלֹהִים אֶת הָאוֹר כִּי טוֹב" הוי במעשיהן של צדיקים חפץ ואינו חפץ במעשיהן של רשעים.

english.text: Rabbi Abahu and Rabbi Ḥiyya the Great, Rabbi Abahu said: Right from the beginning of the creation of the world, the Holy One blessed be He foresaw the actions of the righteous and the actions of the wicked. That is what is written: “For the Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish” (Psalms 1:6). “The earth was emptiness and disorder” – these are the actions of the wicked. “God said: Let there be light” – these are the actions of the righteous. But I do not know which He desires, whether it is the actions of these, or the actions of those. When it is written: “God saw the light, that it was good” (Genesis 1:4) – this shows that He desires the actions of the righteous, and does not desire the actions of the wicked.

notes: The moral reading built as an argument rather than asserted. R. Abahu takes the opening verses as a foresight of the deeds of the righteous and of the wicked — tohu va-vohu the deeds of the wicked, 'let there be light' the deeds of the righteous — and then stops on the difficulty: 'but I do not know which of them he desires.' The verse that settles it is Gen 1:4. Because it is written 'and God saw the light, that it was good', and not written of the darkness, he desires the deeds of the righteous and does not desire the deeds of the wicked. The whole weight falls on what the verse omits to say, which is precisely Augustine's argument in City of God XI.20 and the question Wigbod's pupil asks in his master's face.
